newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Bank Negara braces for fresh attack on ringgit.
newsitem.headline: Bank Negara braces for fresh attack on ringgit.

text.p: Malaysia's central bank is bracing for a fresh speculative attack on the ringgit, widely perceived to be vulnerable in the wake of the Thai baht crisis, dealers and analysts said on Friday.
They said Bank Negara Malaysia could impose foreign exchange controls and continue to actively participate in the market to ward off the possible attack by speculators.
The central bank could not be reached for comment. It also does not usually comment on its open market operations.
The dealers said a new attack on the Malaysian currency looked imminent as speculators were building up long ringgit positions on the swaps.
Such positions would allow speculators to sell ringgit without worrying about being squeezed by the central bank.
The possibility of Bank Negara imposing capital controls was strengthened by market talk that central bank officials will meet chief executive officers of local banks on Saturday.
Dealers believe the meeting is a follow-up to last month's meeting in which the authorities expressed their concern over local banks' active involvement in the forward market.
"The meeting could involve the implementation of some sort of forex controls," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. "It is a likely move after what happened in Thailand."

At the previous meeting, Bank Negara was believed to have told banks, which have high exposure to swaps, that if they continue to deal with speculators, the central bank would not help them at times when they need ringgit.
A restriction on the ringgit forwards would effectively create a two-tier market, like the one in Thailand, by segregating offshore and domestic markets.
Officials at Bank Negara were not immediately available for comment on the meeting.
Talk of the capital controls sent swap rates soaring since Thursday, with one-month swaps up at 100 points from 17 and six-month at 270/300 from 160.
Dealers said there was some perception that speculators would turn their attention to the ringgit after having achieved some partial gains on the Thai baht.
The baht was sold down heavily on Wednesday after the Bank of Thailand announced a baht float.
But some analysts expressed doubts over possible capital controls in Malaysia.
"Malaysia is not like Thailand, so there's no need for a two-tier market in Malaysia," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore. "I think Bank Negara has done well in defending the ringgit."
Dealers said Bank Negara could have sold an estimated $300 million this week to defend the ringgit at 2.5250 to a dollar.
On Wednesday, Bank Negara intervened in the foreign exchange market using its own name for the first time in many years instead of its usual practice of using a broker or a bank.
The ringgit was quoted at 2.5240/50 a dollar at 0600 GMT.
Research house I.D.E.A. said capital controls in Malaysia were definitely out of the question.
It said Malaysian authorities were still looking towards a full financial liberalisation after the year 2000.
"Capital control is actually digging graves for the upcoming financial products," I.D.E.A. said in a report.
In 1994, faced with an attack on the ringgit, Bank Negara imposed negative interest rates on foreign deposits, banned swaps and stopped foreigners from buying Malaysian government paper.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
